newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Fresh report of murder by Kabila troops.
newsitem.headline: Fresh report of murder by Kabila troops.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency on Tuesday urged Congo President Laurent Kabila and the Organisation of African Unity summit to take steps to protect Rwandan refugees after a Save the Children worker and four refugees were killed.

Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) was suspending its aid work at Karuba, near Goma in the Democratic Republic of Congo (formerly Zaire), where Alliance soldiers reportedly carried out the shooting on May 29.
The victims' bodies have not been found in the remote area, but UNHCR said it had no reason to doubt the report pieced together by the London-based aid group.
"Save the Children say that local reports suggest the attackers were part of the military. They describe them as AFDL," O'Toole said, referring to the former rebel Alliance.
"Some elements of the military appear to be out of control and need to be brought under control before any more lives are lost", she told a news briefing.

"Such reports only underline the need for an independent international inquiry into allegations of human rights abuses in the area. We would call on both President Kabila and the Organisation of African Unity summit to take measures to protect refugees and ensure that law and order is upheld in the Democratic Republic of Congo," the spokeswoman added.

The incident was the latest to tarnish the image of Kabila's soldiers amid increasingly vocal calls for his government to cooperate with an independent international inquiry into allegations of massive abuses.
A team of U.N. human rights investigators last month were refused entry into the country to inspect mass graves in the east. They are due to report to the General Assembly by June 30.

Reports of violence against Rwandan Hutus have continued since Kabila's Tutsi-dominated army took Kinshasa last month and drove out former President Mobutu Sese Seko, ending a seven-month military campaign plagued by reported killings.
"This is only the latest in a series of shocking reports of widespread killings or other human rights abuses across the Democratic Republic of Congo, many in the Kivu area," she said.
Two expatriate staff of the U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) were attacked in their home in Goma on May 12 by armed men who bayoneted and terrorised them. Kabila's soldiers were blamed.

O'Toole said: "Such reports have continued since the new government took over in Kinshasa and have been the focus of growing international attention. Many of the allegations centre on areas to which we and other international aid organisations have no access."
The U.N. Security Council last Thursday called for an immediate end to violence against the exiles.

The refugees are remnants of 1.1 million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Some 814,807 have returned home since last November, while 46,300 have been found and about 246,893 remain unaccounted for, according to UNHCR.
In Kinshasa on Monday, Information Minister Raphael Ghenda said there was no proof Rwandan refugees were being massacred.

Save the Children, in a statement issued late on Monday in London, identified the slain local worker as Katumbo Mburanumwe, a social work assistant with its programme which tries to trace refugee families and reunite them with unaccompanied children.
He was taking a group of 11 unaccompanied Rwandan children for repatriation when the attack occurred. A child in his arms and two male adults and one female were the other victims.

Karuba is a major collection point about 45 km (30 miles) west of Goma, where refugees gather on their way home after hiding out in the forest around Masisi and Walikale. About 25,000 people went through Karuba in March and April, although O'Toole said numbers had dropped to a trickle since the attack.

"The suspension will affect both our repatriation work and rehabilitation projects in the area. It will last as long as it takes to get assurances that we and other aid agencies can work in the area with security and without being harassed," she said.
